152.stem:
In a bag there are 3 six-sided dice. Two of the dice have faces marked 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The other is a special die with faces marked 1, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5.

One die is randomly selected and tossed.

parts.latex: What is the probability that the die shows a 5?
Given that the die shows a 5, what is the probability that it is the special die?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(5) &= \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{18} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{special die} \mid 5) &= \dfrac{P(\text{special die} \cap 5)}{P(5)} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{6}}{\frac{5}{18}} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$

200.stem:
Four Year 12 students want to organise a graduation party. All four students have the same probability, $P(F)$, of being available next Friday. All four students have the same probability, $P(S)$, of being available next Saturday.

It is given that $P(F)=\dfrac{3}{10}$, $P(S\mid F)=\dfrac{1}{3}$, and $P(F\mid S)=\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Kim is one of the four students.

parts.latex: Is Kim's availability next Friday independent from his availability next Saturday? Justify your answer.
Show that the probability that Kim is available next Saturday is $\dfrac{4}{5}$.
What is the probability that at least one of the four students is NOT available next Saturday?

solutions.latex: No, since $P(F\mid S)\ne P(F)$.

$$\begin{aligned}P(S\mid F)&=\dfrac{P(S\cap F)}{P(F)}\\\dfrac{1}{3}&=\dfrac{P(S\cap F)}{\frac{3}{10}}\\P(S\cap F)&=\dfrac{1}{10}\\P(F\mid S)&=\dfrac{P(S\cap F)}{P(S)}\\\dfrac{1}{8}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{10}}{P(S)}\qquad\left(\text{since }P(S\cap F)=P(F\cap S)\right)\\P(S)&=\dfrac{8}{10}\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use conditional probability formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}1-\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^4&=1-\dfrac{256}{625}\\&=\dfrac{369}{625}\\&=0.5904\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: A bag contains six white socks and eight black socks. Two socks are selected at random without replacement. Given the two selected socks are the same colour, which of the following is the closest to the probability that they are both black?

parts.latex: A die is rolled twice. Let events $X$ and $Y$ be: $$X=\{\text{The first roll is a }'1'\}$$ $$Y=\{\text{Sum of two rolls is }'7'\}$$ Which of the following statements is true?

solutions.latex:
There are $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$P(X)=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac16$$
A sum of $7$ comes from $(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)$, so
$$P(Y)=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac16$$
Both events happen only for $(1,6)$, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\cap Y)&=\dfrac{1}{36}\\ &=\dfrac16\times\dfrac16\\ &=P(X)\times P(Y) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

($X$ and $Y$ can both happen, so they are not mutually exclusive; $X$ is not a subset of $Y$; $P(X)=P(Y)$.)

662.stem:
A bag contains 3 white and 4 black stones. Two stones are drawn out of the bag with the probability tree below showing the possibilities:

\exfigure{1370_q4_1}

figures.cap: probability tree for drawing two stones: white 3/7, black 4/7, then 2/6, 4/6, 3/6, 3/6

parts.latex: If it is known that one of the stones is white, what is the probability that the stones are different colours?

'At least one' probabilities.reason: Conditioning event is at least one white, found as 1 - P(none).

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability, $P(X\mid Y)=\dfrac{P(X\cap Y)}{P(Y)}$, where "one of the stones is white" means at least one white:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one white})&=1-\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{30}{42}\\ P(\text{different colours})&=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{6}+\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{24}{42} \end{aligned}$$
Different colours always includes one white stone, so
$$P(\text{different}\mid\text{one white})=\dfrac{24}{42}\div\dfrac{30}{42}=\dfrac{4}{5}$$

795.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\overline{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram with complement-of-A intersect B shaded

parts.latex: Find the expression of $P(A\cap B)$ in terms of $k$.
Given that the two events are independent, find the value of $k$.

solutions.latex:
The events are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$. Using (a):
$$\begin{aligned} k-k^2 &= \dfrac{3k}{4}\cdot k\\ 4k-4k^2 &= 3k^2\\ 7k^2-4k &= 0\\ k(7k-4) &= 0\\ k &= 0 \text{ or } k=\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$k=0$ is not allowed since $0<k<1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{4}{7}$$
criteria: Uses $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The probability that Young's soccer team wins this weekend is $\dfrac{4}{9}$. The probability that Young's rugby league team wins this weekend is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

What is the probability that neither team wins this weekend?

solutions.latex:
Let $S$ be "soccer team wins" and $R$ be "rugby team wins". The results are independent, so multiply the complements:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(\overline{S}\cap\overline{R}\right)&=\left(1-\dfrac{4}{9}\right)\times\left(1-\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\\&=\dfrac{5}{9}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=\dfrac{5}{36}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are two chance events such that $P(A)=0.45$, $P(B)=0.3$ and $P(A|B)=0.6$.

What is the value of $P(B|A)$?

solutions.latex:
Using $P(B\cap A)=P(A|B)\times P(B)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(B|A)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{P(A|B)\times P(B)}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{0.6\times0.3}{0.45}\\&=0.4\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are two independent events with $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{5}{8}$ and $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{6}$.

What is the value of $P(B)$?

solutions.latex:
By the addition rule, $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.

$A$ and $B$ are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)\left[1-P(A)\right]\\ \dfrac{5}{8}&=\dfrac{1}{6}+P(B)\left[1-\dfrac{1}{6}\right]\\ \dfrac{5}{8}-\dfrac{1}{6}&=P(B)\times\dfrac{5}{6}\\ \dfrac{15-4}{24}&=P(B)\times\dfrac{5}{6}\\ P(B)&=\dfrac{11}{24}\times\dfrac{6}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{11}{20} \end{aligned}$$

900.stem:
Four students want to organise a netball game. All four students have the same probability, $P(T)$, of being available next Tuesday. All four students have the same probability, $P(W)$, of being available next Wednesday. Josie is one of the four students.

It is known that $P(T)=\dfrac{2}{5}$, $P(W\mid T)=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(T\mid W)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

parts.latex: Is Josie's availability next Tuesday independent from her availability next Wednesday? Justify your answer.
Show that the probability that Josie is available next Wednesday is $\dfrac{3}{10}$.
What is the probability that at least one of the four students is NOT available next Wednesday?

solutions.latex:
If $T$ and $W$ are independent, then $P(T\mid W)=P(T)$ and $P(W\mid T)=P(W)$.

But $P(T\mid W)=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $P(T)=\dfrac{2}{5}$.

$\therefore P(T\mid W)\ne P(T)$

$\therefore T$ and $W$ are \underline{not} independent.

Using $P(W\mid T)=\dfrac{P(W\cap T)}{P(T)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{4}&=\dfrac{P(W\cap T)}{\frac{2}{5}}\\ P(W\cap T)&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{20}=\dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$
Using $P(T\mid W)=\dfrac{P(T\cap W)}{P(W)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{10}}{P(W)}\\ P(W)&=\dfrac{1}{10}\div\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{10}\times\dfrac{3}{1}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

"At least one not available" is the complement of "all four available", and the students are independent:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-P(\text{all available on }W)&=1-\left(\dfrac{3}{10}\right)^4\\ &=1-\dfrac{81}{10\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{9919}{10\,000} \end{aligned}$$

986.stem:
Joe plays soccer, a sport where a team can win, lose or draw.

Joe is prone to injury, and misses $20\%$ of his team's games.

When Joe plays, his team has a $77\%$ chance of winning and a $10\%$ chance of losing.

When Joe does not play, his team has a $53\%$ chance of winning and a $25\%$ chance of losing.

figures.cap: solution sketch: tree diagram: J 0.8 (W 0.77, D 0.13, L 0.1), J-bar 0.2 (W 0.53, D 0.22, L 0.25)

parts.latex: Calculate the probability that Joe's team loses any given game.
Given that Joe's team does not lose in a particular match, what is the probability that Joe played in that match?

criteria: Identifies all possible outcomes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When Joe plays, the team does not lose with probability $0.77+0.13=0.9$ (win or draw).

Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(J\mid\bar{L}\right)&=\dfrac{P\left(J\cap\bar{L}\right)}{P\left(\bar{L}\right)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.8\times(0.77+0.13)}{1-0.13}\\ &=\dfrac{24}{29}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies all possible outcomes, or equivalent merit

1483.stem: Sixty people visited a swimming pool one afternoon. Thirteen out of the twenty-three people who wore goggles were adults. There were nineteen children.

parts.latex:
Complete the two-way table below, showing this information.

\extable{335_q20_t1}
If an adult is selected at random, what is the probability they were wearing goggles?

An additional group of adults, not wearing goggles, arrived at the pool.

The probability that a person selected at random is an adult who is not wearing goggles is now 0.6.

How many additional adults arrived?

solutions.latex: \extable{Ts2175_1}
criteria: Completes the table with up to three errors, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
There are $60-19=41$ adults, 13 of whom wore goggles.
$$P(\text{goggles}\mid\text{adult})=\dfrac{13}{41}$$

Let $x$ be the number of additional adults.

There are $41-13=28$ adults not wearing goggles, and $60+x$ people in total.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{adult not wearing goggles})&=\dfrac{28+x}{60+x}\\ \dfrac{3}{5}&=\dfrac{28+x}{60+x}\\ 3(60+x)&=5(28+x)\\ 180+3x&=140+5x\\ 40&=2x\\ x&=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 20 additional adults arrived.
criteria: Finds an expression for $P(\text{adult not wearing goggles})$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A bag contains eight cards that are each printed with one of the following sets of characters.

$$\text{aaa}\qquad\text{aab}\qquad\text{aba}\qquad\text{baa}\qquad\text{abb}\qquad\text{bab}\qquad\text{bba}\qquad\text{bbb}$$

A student chooses one card at random.

Let $N_1$ be the event that the first character printed on the card is an ‘a’ and $N_2$ be the event that the first and second characters printed on the card are both an ‘a’.

Determine whether $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events.

solutions.latex:
$N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent if $P(N_1\cap N_2)=P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(N_1)&=\dfrac{4}{8}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ P(N_2)&=\dfrac{2}{8}=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ P(N_1\cap N_2)&=\dfrac{2}{8}=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ P(N_1)\times P(N_2)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{8}\end{aligned}$$
$P(N_1)\times P(N_2)\ne P(N_1\cap N_2)$

$\therefore\ N_1$ and $N_2$ are not independent.
criteria: Finds $P(N_1\cap N_2)=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$, or equivalent merit

A bag contains six cards that are each printed with one of the following numbers.

$$111,\ 121,\ 122,\ 211,\ 221,\ 222$$

A student chooses one card at random.

Let $N_1$ be the event that the first digit of the number on the card is 1, and $N_2$ be the event that the second digit of the number on the card is 1.

Determine whether $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}N_1&=\{111,121,122\}\\ N_2&=\{111,211\}\\ N_1\cap N_2&=\{111\}\end{aligned}$$
Each of the 6 cards is equally likely:
$$P(N_1)=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad P(N_2)=\dfrac{1}{3},\quad P(N_1\cap N_2)=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
If $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events, then $P(N_1\cap N_2)=P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(N_1)\times P(N_2)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\\ &=P(N_1\cap N_2)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent.
criteria: Compares $P(N_1\cap N_2)$ with $P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A flood insurance company determines that N, the number of claims received in a month, is a random variable with

$$P(N=n)=\dfrac{2}{3^{n+1}},\ \text{for } n=0,1,2,\ldots.$$

The numbers of claims received in different months are independent.

In any consecutive two-month period, calculate the probability that more than one claim will be received, given that zero claims were received at least one of the two months.

solutions.latex:
From $P(N=n)=\dfrac{2}{3^{n+1}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(N=0)&=\dfrac{2}{3} \\ P(N=1)&=\dfrac{2}{9} \\ P(N\ge2)&=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Solution 1:

\exfigure{361_q34_s1}
$$P(\text{at least one month with zero claims})=1-\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
More than one claim in total, given a zero month, means one month has zero claims and the other has $2$ or more:
$$\begin{aligned} P(N>1\mid\text{at least one zero month})&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{9}}{\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{4}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Solution 2:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\dfrac{P(0)P(0)+P(0)P(1)+P(1)P(0)}{P(0,0)+P(0,n)+P(n,0)} \\ &=1-\dfrac{\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{9}+\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=1-\dfrac{\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly recognises the sum of three combination events in the numerator, or equivalent merit

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent events where $P(X)=0.2$ and $P(Y)=0.52$

What is the value of $P(\bar{X}\cap\bar{Y})$ ?

solutions.latex:
$X$ and $Y$ are independent, so $\bar X$ and $\bar Y$ are also independent.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar X\cap\bar Y) &= P(\bar X)\times P(\bar Y) \\ &= (1-0.2)(1-0.52) \\ &= 0.8\times 0.48 \\ &= 0.384 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.
